newsitem.title: PERU: Dim hopes for quick renewal of Peru hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Dim hopes for quick renewal of Peru hostage talks.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis, nearing its 100th day, held out only a dim hope on Monday for a renewal soon of direct talks between President Alberto Fujimori's government and leftist rebels holding 72 hostages.

The country's Roman Catholic primate, Archbishop Augusto Vargas Alzamora, urged both sides to loosen their demands and resume face-to-face talks aimed at settling the 97-day takeover at the Japanese ambassador's residence peacefully.

"I think this must end soon," Vargas told reporters after a Palm Sunday service in which he called for remembrance of the 72 hostages under the gun of submachinegun-toting rebels in the Japanese ambassador's house.
"We can't continue with this bickering attitude. I think that among both sides, there are positions that need to be relaxed -- tough and inflexible attitudes," he said.

Suspected guerrillas commandered a police pickup truck in Lima's eastern outskirts on Sunday night and killed the two officers driving it, making off with their automatic rifles, bulletproof vests and a revolver, police said.

The shooting, which bore all the hallmarks of a guerrilla attack, would be the most serious rebel attack in Lima since the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels took over the Japanese residence on Dec. 17, 1996.
It was not immediately clear if the attack was the work of MRTA or another group, the Maoist Shining Path, which is more active in the working-class outskirts of Lima.
Vargas' statements reflected growing impatience among the Peruvian public with the siege, which began when MRTA rebels blasted into a cocktail party and took all the guests hostage.

Talks to free the captives began in late December but have been at a near-standstill since early this month, with only one face-to-face meeting in the past 18 days as talks stalled on the MRTA's demand of freedom for about 450 jailed comrades.
Fujimori, whose brother Pedro and two cabinet ministers are among the hostages, has flatly rejected the demand.

Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura, back in Tokyo after a trip to Lima followed by visits to Cuba and the Dominican Republic to arrange asylum for the hostage-takers, said he believed the time was ripe to end the standoff.
"The situation may appear deadlocked at first sight, but I am convinced that the issue is heading towards a solution," Komura told reporters. "I think the time is ripe for a peaceful settlement."
With Peru and the rest of the Roman Catholic world entering Holy Week, appeals for the freedom of the hostages took a religious tone as the Catholic faithful tried to lift their spirits.

Parishioners from a working-class Lima district wore biblical costumes and held a procession, complete with palm fronds and a man dressed as Jesus riding a donkey near the mansion in a Sunday show of support for the hostages.
"We ask for forgiveness for the captors and freedom for the hostages," said Mario Valencia, 36, who played Jesus.

He led about 60 people playing the roles of shepherds, the Three Kings, Mary, Joseph and other religious figures, down streets surrounding the diplomatic compound reciting passages from the New Testament.
Hostages have spent Christmas and New Year's as captives of about 20 rebels, some of them teenagers, and appear likely to spend Easter, next Sunday, that way too.

Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a mediator in the tense standoff between security forces and the MRTA, entered the home, towing a suitcase behind him, and spent two hours inside apparently delivering mass.

Local news media and analysts have painted a gloomy picture of efforts to end the standoff, some speculating that the slow pace of talks could strengthen the hand of those in Fujimori's government who would use force.
"The situation is one of total apathy," political analyst Raul Gonzales said.
